The NKRCP encompasses 1,993,075 hectares (4.7 million acres) of grassland in northern Kenya (Pinette, 2024). It is the world�s largest soil carbon removal project managed by the NRT, a non-governmental organization that initiated conservation work in the 1990s. They advocate for community-based conservancies (CBCs), facilitate their management, and promote planned grazing and the conservation of wildlife corridors and forests in Kenya and Uganda. NRT has 44 community conservancies in Kenya, most of which are in northern Kenya, where inhabitants are nomadic pastoralists who share the environment with wildlife. The project that began in 2012 was approved in 2021 by the Verified Carbon Standard (VCS), a program that credits greenhouse gas (GHS) projects and is run by Vera. This non-profit institution manages and develops standards for climate action, responsible business practices, sustainable development and the Climate, Community & Biodiversity Alliance (CCBA) standards. The benefiting CBCs are situated in Laikipia County, Marsabit County, Samburu County, and Isiolo County (see Figure 1).Figure 1: Map of NRT Carbon project area within Laikipia, Samburu, Isiolo and Marsabit Counties in Northern Kenya. modified from (Owino et al., forthcoming)
The empirical data presented here is part of 75 in-depth interviews and focus group discussions with stakeholders in Samburu and Isiolo County based on 11 months of fieldwork between 2022 and 2024 within 8 of the 14 carbon credit sites under the NRT governance in northern Kenya.

The NKRCP operation entails a rotational grazing pattern different from pastoral communities' traditional animal husbandry. The project monitors the net methane (CH4) from traditional pastoral livestock activities. It implements a rotational grazing pattern, assisting in storing carbon in the soil and recovering perennial grassland. The project will be implemented for 30 years from 2021 and is currently estimated to positively impact 175,000 nomadic pastoral lives (NRT, n.d.). It is assumed that it provides a novel economic intervention that can reduce environmental pressures by incentivizing sustainable land management (NRT, 2022).Using the double exposure lens, the main question I probe is: �To what extent are the losers in climate change also the losers when it comes to economic globalisation?� (O�Brien and Leichenko, 2000). Political ecologists developed this approach to understand the simultaneous effects of climate change and globalization on regions, communities, and ecosystems. It exposes carbon credits as a double-edged sword, where excessive rain and droughts brought on by climate change intersect with a changing financial landscape in the globalized economy through trade liberalization and increased foreign investments.

Vulnerable communities often lack the capacity to cope with this kind of double pressure, and this usually leads to a worsening of their standard of living and increased economic vulnerabilities unless mitigated by targeted interventions (Evite and Zara, 2023). While carbon credits provide financial incentivization to local communities for maintaining rangelands, swamps or forests to store more carbon and help mitigate climate change, they have proven to pose potential risks of exacerbating resource-based conflicts due to abrupt and large-scale land-use changes and restriction policies that socially and economically affect local communities in marginalized regions. Thus, critics of climate finance argue that it is a mechanism that promotes neocolonialism in the Global South because it is an initiative funded by the Global North (Evite and Zara, 2023). The argument is that the commodification of natural resources, often through carbon credit schemes, has led to unprecedented land use and ownership shifts. This has exacerbated resource-based conflicts in these regions as the authority over land has gone into the hands of private businesses at the frontier and out of the hands of the state (Bersaglio, 2017; Lohmann 2008). These disruptions affect traditional livelihoods and create dependency on profit-oriented external markets from carbon credits.Northern Kenya's Historical and Current Conflict Dynamics
Today�s northern Kenya, formerly known as the Northern Frontier District (NFD), was established during British colonial rule in 1925. It covers a vast area inhabited primarily by pastoralist communities. Throughout the colonial period, the NFD was administered separately from the rest of the country, a policy driven by its perceived remoteness and security concerns related to the region�s proximity to Ethiopia and Somalia (Schlee, 2013). Following a failed attempt to join Somalia after Kenya�s independence in 1963, the NFD has coped with a legacy of neglect, marginalization, and contested identity to date (Sharamo, 2014).

Northern Kenya has long been characterized by violent conflicts, particularly among pastoral groups. Using the ACLED (Armed Conflict Location and Event Data) to analyze pastoral conflicts in the last five years, Figure 2 illustrates the fluctuation in lethal events�at least one person killed, the number of conflict events involving pastoral actors and the resulting fatalities. Conflict incidents intensified, and lethal conflicts also showed a substantial increase. This is partly tied to the prolonged drought that affected northern Kenya between 2018 to 2023, suggesting a correlation between environmental-induced challenges that enhanced the mobility of pastoralists and intensifying conflicts over scarce resources. The 2007 conflict also shows the post-election violence that affected the whole country. Traditional ethnic rivalries, the need to restock livestock after drought or disease, and cultural practices such as revenge, supremacy battles, and bride price payments continue to play a role (Witsenburg and Adano, 2014). More recent factors include boundary-making conflicts caused by ethnically defined counties since 2013.Devolution is pushing for defined county boundaries, escalating ethnic mobilization and politicization of ethnicity. These new dynamics, combined with the commercialization of livestock rustling, have intensified resource competition as fighting is focused on access and control, and boundaries seem to be a tool that can enable access or limit one community against accessing resources across inter-county borderlands (Eaton, 2010; Schilling et al. 2012). Critical pastoral resources such as livestock, water, land, and pasture are central to these conflicts. These resources are all affected by environmental pressures, including droughts, floods, and increasing variability in the region�s two major rainy seasons, April and October (Eberle et al., 2019).In Northern Kenya, while climate-related resource scarcity, such as the prolonged drought, affects the timing and frequency of raids, governance of these resources in the newly devolved system, are critical in determining whether resource depletion leads to conflict or more cooperation. With NRT through conservation initiatives, conflicts intensified following conservancies' expansion and commercialized raids1 it is involving local warriors and NRT rangers. The NGO has been condemned by local communities as an agent of violence following the extrajudicial killings of local pastoralists, even though the NRT promotes itself as an agent of peace by defining its work in conservation as peacebuilding (Counsell, 2023).The Unintended Consequences of NKRCP in their Attempt to �Sell Pastoral Air�
The Natural Solution Climate Alliance (NSCA) and President William Ruto, during the COP27 climate conference in 20222, presented NKRCP as a crucial and timely initiative to combat climate change through carbon sequestration while promoting biodiversity and sustainable rangeland use for wildlife and pastoralists. However, beneath the environmental solution agenda lies a problematic complex of social inequalities and violent contestations stemming from restricted grazing policies and the exclusion of pastoralists from carbon financial benefits3. The reallocation of traditional communal grazing lands for carbon sequestration zones within Borana and Samburu land turned into a violent invasion in 2023 when young morans (unmarried warriors)4, armed with rifles, felt they had no choice but to forcefully access core conservation areas preserved for wildlife and tourist lodges to access pasture for their livestock. Within the carbon methodology, the idea that pastoralists historically depended on the ability to move across vast landscapes in search of water and pasture for their livestock has been completely ignored. Mobility is essential for their survival as resources were shared in times of severe environmental scarcity, which has been disrupted by the carbon credit model of preserving rangelands for carbon storage in the soil (Mkutu, 2008).Some interviewees expressed frustrations following the restriction policies that exacerbated existing vulnerabilities. Especially during the prolonged drought from 2018 to 2023, which swept almost 80% of pastoral livestock in northern Kenya, the need for pasture was urgent (see the spike of conflicts from Figure 2 above). The exclusion from these grazing lands was perceived as a loss of economic livelihood and a violation of customary land rights5. The situation worsened insecurity and often pushed the state to deploy police officers to protect tourist facilities from local invasions6. Between 2022, when carbon funds were dispatched to conservancies, and 2023, NRT spent more resources and time on peacebuilding activities following a spike of violence in conservancies rather than using those funds for pastoral development. These areas are now converted to tourism sites with expensive lodges that locals cannot access or afford, even for manual labor. They are also defined as core conservation areas for wildlife, blocking the pastoral communities. This led to tensions among the locals who felt disenfranchised by the carbon project, placing international markets over the well-being of the locals and the survival of their culture and livelihood for future generations7. As one of the elders representing the Borana community in Isiolo statedwe have a traditional system of managing rangeland known as the dedha system,�NRT demonized this as an �unplanned� way of managing rangeland; hence, they brought a �planned� rotational grazing that only allows us to graze in one place for a maximum of three weeks�This has undermined our Indigenous knowledge that we fear is now viewed as primitive, and the hidden agenda here is to deny us access to land and grab it�this carbon agenda is a scam of the decade�they are using our name to get money, and nothing comes to the communityMoreover, inequalities have been exacerbated by the way carbon revenues are distributed. As NRT and international partners like The Nature Conservancy benefit from carbon sales, the local pastoralists reap limited or no financial rewards. For instance, NRT disclosed that in 2022 and 2023, each of the 14 conservancies received US$324,000 per conservancy from carbon sales (Ndirangu, 2024). According to the NRT bylaws, the funds should be directed through the conservancy managers, who work with the board members to make decisions for the community regarding which projects or issues to focus resources on and support the conservancy members. However, the locals interviewed felt sidelined from the decision-making process, resulting in increased mistrust, frustration and suspicion about the true beneficiaries of carbon funds. The pastoralists interviewed claimed that the process is top-down and institutionalized, fearing there is no transparency in what NRT gets from the �sale of their air�9.

Interviewees also pointed to systemic issues within conservancies, as unequal distribution of carbon revenues reinforces existing social hierarchies because elites closely supported by politicians and economic power structures benefit disproportionately from carbon credit sales. It was noted that some board members and managers are accused of mismanaging funds, and there are reports of political interference and manipulation during elections for conservancy chairpersons making it a lucrative position to die for10. This is because elites often control resources channeled to manage development within conservancies. They allegedly use their positions, power, and influence for personal gain, excluding the broader community from the benefits. The sidelining of pastoralist voices fuels resentment and perpetuates further marginalization in a region grappling with historical neglect policies stemming from colonial and post-colonial regimes that have not been addressed to date11. Ethnic rivalries, governance challenges, and limited access to development further complicate these resource-based conflicts12.

According to Survival International (Blood Carbon report) of 202313, the NKRCP project design should have considered the Indigenous knowledge systems and priorities of pastoralists who own land and resources. Locals also affirmed this during the interviews. Some respondents felt that the promise of long-term environmental sustainability through carbon credits was too abstract for local needs and realities. These specifically stemmed from grazing committees and councils of elders unaware of where the carbon revenues disappeared after being released by NRT to the conservancy managers14. Many stated that they are left in the dark as no one has ever called for a public participation meeting per the Kenyan constitution to decide on projects appropriate for pastoralists, as few elites decide on their behalf what they think is best for the community. Another significant issue concerning the concept of the carbon project is the gap in understanding about what carbon is and how it is measured, how it operates, and where it is sold. Pastoralists interviewed could not fully grasp the concept of carbon trading. To them, they know NRT is �selling their air� or �Suwo� (as the Samburu call it)15. This has led to confusion, rumors, and mistrust as some were skeptical of taking the money, alluding to it as dirty/blood money because selling air is like selling ghosts16.

Some communities also acknowledged receiving benefits such as scholarships and bursaries for their children, water projects, and employment of rangers in conservancies. However, the general sentiment is that these benefits are unevenly distributed throughout northern Kenya, which is conserving its rangelands. The issue of corruption and emerging carbon millionaires who are conservancy managers is becoming a concern17. The perception is that a significant amount of money is being funneled into private hands rather than shared equitably by the communities doing the rangeland management work18. When carbon was implemented, the pastoral communities had higher expectations and aspirations, hoping to improve their livelihoods. Although the project was initially perceived as a potential source of wealth and development, the reality has disappointed many pastoralists19.Conclusion
The surge of capitalist nature-based solution projects such as carbon credits poses a risk of escalating natural resource conflicts, especially in the Global South, where rangelands, forests and swamps are targeted and converted in the name of invasive and expansive activities such as carbon offset schemes (Weldemichel, 2022). The findings reveal that climate finance initiatives, such as carbon markets, offer new economic opportunities to empower Indigenous communities' livelihoods. They have proven that they also limit control, access, and use of critical resources like rangelands for pastoralist groups in northern Kenya. This complicates traditional resource-sharing mechanisms by the pastoral communities, whose ethnic or county boundaries have never been delimited. The carbon project poses the risk of dispossession of pastoralists from their ancestral lands, amplifying resource competition by creating scarcity in fragile ecologies prone to climate variabilities. Several communities had to alter traditional grazing patterns due to climate variability and newly imposed land management policies under the carbon sequestration project promoted by NRT. For communities that have faced marginalization and underdevelopment for decades from colonial to post-colonial regimes in Kenya, the carbon project is seen as another form of invasion and alienation of Indigenous land.External entrepreneurs impose carbon credit interventions that do not serve pastoralists� interests nor address their urgent realities and needs. The entanglement of harsh environmental changes, natural resource exploitation and restrictions, and social inequalities intensifies competition over shrinking resources. These communities are already locked in ethnic rivalries and resource-based conflicts. They are now experiencing the new dilemma of greater polarization as restrictions on land are viewed through the lens of carbon colonialism. Additionally, the intensification and expansion of conservation efforts in northern Kenya continue to pose further challenges produced by international actors� capitalist-driven motives, the lack of genuine community involvement, the missing action of the Kenya government in protecting the vulnerable communities, the inadequate devolution of conservation landscapes, and ongoing resource conflicts. These issues undermine carbon markets� professed sustainable environment, wildlife conservation, and equitable and sustainable development goals. The findings have shown that the NKRCP exemplifies a double exposure tragedy in that pastoral communities grapple with the double-edged frontier of climate-induced environmental changes and the commodification of capitalist appropriation of natural resources.

7. Rights to carbon, and benefits from the project7.1 Consent, consultation and information provision The evidence that prior and informed consent for the project was obtained from the relevant communities � or even the conservancy management regimes � is ambiguous. There are also
questions about whether the legal right to trade the carbon was properly obtained before such trading began. The project document of 2020 noted that;�The carbon project�has been communicated much more recently due to high uncertainty in the carbon market and a reluctance to raise hopes about potential revenues�115 (emphasis added). It further stated that; �the Conservancies began on 15 May 2015 a solicitation of participation and public comment period, with announcement and information about the project distributed by NRT grazing coordinators and other staff in the form of pamphlets�.116 It should be noted that May 2015 is two and a half years after the project started. The project also stated that �stakeholders� would be informed through a �soon-to-be posted announcement on the NRT website (http://nrtkenya.org ) plus the front pages of each Conservancy linked to a blog site (http://nrtcarbonproject.wordpress.com ) where the announcement also exists and anyone can post comments anonymously about it�117. This latter website is still open and, as of February 2023, is completely devoid of content (see Figure 14 below).The project document then goes on to say that �These announcements were followed by community meetings in September and October 2016, open to all members in each Conservancy, in each of the 13 participating Conservancies�119. This round of announcements and meetings took place almost at the very end of the first four-year verification and crediting period. Side-stepping the issue of whether the communications and meetings provided consent for the carbon project or indeed addressed the specifics of it, the project noted that �In the meetings, community grazing committee chairmen communicated how grazing plans had been implemented or not in the past and reviewed past compliance with grazing plans, identified barriers to compliance, and communicated expected benefits of project activities as rotational or migratory grazing. The response of communities, especially after September 2016 meetings and workshops were improved efforts to make, write, and implement grazing plans within Conservancies. This provides evidence that community members understood the benefits of project activities and approved intensified efforts to conduct grazing plans.�120
The validation of the project accepted that pamphlets had been submitted to the communities, but also noted that: �at the time of the site visit the local language summaries of the P[roject] D[document] and P[roject] I[mplementation] R[eport] did not appear to have been distributed. When discussed with the project proponent they stated that the documents would be distributed after the site visit, and photographic evidence would be provided that all communities were reached121.  In September 2015, the validators then requested the project to �Please provide evidence (i.e. date
stamped georeferenced photos) that the PD and PIR ha have been posted and made available to all communities� 122. Following receipt from the project of pictures purporting to show this, the validators then recorded that: �Photographs of what appear to be monitoring report summaries in ten conservancies were provided. Dates ranged widely, and it appears the date of the file is not necessarily the date the picture was taken, as shown by a time stamp on the photo from the Nakuprat Conservancy, which appears to have been taken in January of 2010. No georeferenced information was included in any of the files.�123 The validators do not comment on the fact that evidence for three of the thirteen participating conservancies was not provided at all, nor who exactly within the conservancies was pictured receiving the documents, or whether this in any way represented proper consultation or even provision of information to the wider community, nor whether the photographs demonstrated that the documents were being provided in a local language so as to be intelligible to local people. However, evidently still unconvinced by the photographs, the validators then asked the project again to �Please provide georeferenced photos and provide the dates they were taken�Three years later, the project replied in September 2018 that: �Due to delays in completing the validation, the project has been re-posted for public comment in the project zone (February 15- March 15, 2019) at both Conservancy HQ�s and at public announcement kiosks in major towns and villages. Photos with time stamps and associated GPS are available to the VVB�125 This still does not confirm that the right documents had been provided in the right languages to the right people and whether any of what purportedly and eventually had been done represented a meaningful form of information provision, let alone consultation. Nevertheless, the validators accepted that �Photos with date stamps were provided to satisfy this request of multiple locations where the public comment announcement was posted. The item is addressed�126. Clearly, with information having been provided, at best, only late into the project and possibly not in a form even then suitable for the recipients, it is impossible to conclude that Free Prior and Informed Consent had been granted to the project proponents at the start of the project by the area�s indigenous communities. As evidence of consultation having been carried out, the project referred to a social survey in which: �As part of baseline social data gathering, community elders, women and young herders (morani) were asked a series of questions in focus groups in three Conservancies, and over 1000 households were interviewed in a household survey of four Conservancies in October 2014�127. The validators pointed out that this does not explain �why these individuals are legitimate representatives and does not discuss how the adequate levels of information sharing with the groups take place�. In September 2015 they asked for an explanation of how these individuals were selected and to �Please describe the information flow in the project and how the lower level community members receive and provide information�128. Again, the project took three years to reply, by providing information about how the �focus groups� had been selected. Again, this does not actually explain how consultation was undertaken (rather than a �social survey� to obtain project baseline data) but the validators nevertheless concluded that:
�the project has been able to demonstrate that consultations and participatory processes have been undertaken directly with communities and information sharing with the members.of the groups have occurred. The item is addressed.�129 As with the issues of additionality, baselines and leakage, the clear evidence of non-compliance in terms of information provision and consultation should have been sufficient for Verra to reject the validation carried out by Aster Global.It is worth repeating that this finally �validated� evidence of information provision and consultation being undertaken by the project came nearly six years after the project had started and nearly two years after the first four-year period of carbon crediting had already been completed. As the next section explores, formal agreements to transfer the rights to NRT to trade the carbon came even later. On April 21st, 2020 � two weeks after the validation of the carbon project, but some six months before the first verification - a group of Samburu and Borana Elders took the unusual step of jointly calling for international donors to cease providing funding to, and �totally disassociate� themselves from, NRT over serious violation of human rights130. 7.2 Rights to the carbonThe project document states that �Rights to benefit from soil conservation as a component of
wildlife conservation are conferred by the right to register lands as Conservancies by the Kenya
Wildlife Conservation and Management Act of 2013 and by the recently signed Community
Lands Bill of 2016�131. In fact the former Act contains no reference to soil, even in its definitions
of what constitutes �ecosystems�, �wildlife conservation areas� etc132. The latter law only refers to
soil in relation to the prevention of erosion133. Neither law refers to carbon, carbon projects or the
generation of income from the sale of offsets.
In the validation, the validators requested NRT to:
�Please clarify how NRT is granted ownership through the Kenya Community Land Act of
2016, demonstrating that the Project Proponent has the unconditional, undisputed and
unencumbered ability to claim that the project will or did generate or cause the project�s
climate, community and biodiversity benefits Nowhere in the final 2020 project document
does NRT actually state that it has this right�.134
The project replied that �some communities [seven in number] �exist as or have applied for
registration as Group Ranches� a status which confers rights to hold assets (which, the project
claims, could include soil carbon). The remainder (six) are �located on Trust lands, which confer
rights to grazing and by inference (emphasis added) resources that promote grazing (such as
water, soil carbon) under customary law conferred by Section VIII item 59 of the Kenya Trust Land
Act of 2010For the first group, the repealed Land (Group Representatives) Act provided for land ownership
under group ranch system governed and managed by incorporated group representatives. This
system ceased to exist upon the promulgation of the Constitution of Kenya, 2010, which only
recognized public land, private land, and community land. The Community Land Act of 2016
repealed the Land (Group Representatives) Act and offered provisions guiding the transition to
community land.In regards to conservancies that had already acquired Group Ranch status, Section 47 (3) of
the Community Land Act requires land held by Group Representatives not to be sold, leased,
or converted to private land before it has been registered under the Community Land Act. The
first-ever registration of community land in Kenya was the Il Ngwesi and Mosul communities, and
Sereolipi communities in Samburu County by transitioning their land from Group Ranch status,
these being the only two to achieve this outcome up until 2021.
For the second group, the legal basis of soil carbon ownership is merely inferred from the legal right
to graze. In fact, the Community Land Act 2016, which repealed the Trust Land Act of 2010, places
clear obligations on anyone seeking to utilize or invest in lands deemed to be covered by the Act,
regardless of whether they had been registered or not (so far, no Trust lands within the project area
have been registered136). Section 38 of the Act provides that regulation of community land use and
the management of community land shall be subject to national and county government laws and
policies relating to the exploitation of minerals and natural resources among others � but there is no
substantive law in Kenya, either at the County or national level, enacted to provide a mechanism for
or regulate carbon credit generation or trading. Section 36 of the Act requires that any agreement
relating to an investment in community land shall be made after a free, open consultative process
and shall contain provisions on the following aspects: (a) an environmental, social, cultural and
economic impact assessment; (b) stakeholder consultations and involvement of the community; (c)
continuous monitoring and evaluation of the impact of the investment to the community.
Section 6 (6) of the Community Land Act provides that any transaction in relation to unregistered
community land within the county shall be in accordance with the provisions of this Act and any
other applicable law. Section 36(2) provides that an agreement relating to investment in community
land shall only be made between the investor and the community and that no agreement between
an investor and the community shall be valid unless it is approved by two-thirds of adult members
at a community assembly meeting called to consider the offer and at which a quorum of two-thirds
of the adult members of that community is represented.
There is no evidence that the relevant assessments were undertaken in compliance with the
law, nor that there was a process of consultation as required, nor that two-thirds of community
members approved NRT�s proposed investment of carbon funds, nor that the necessary licenses
were obtained from the respective County Governments.In other words, the legal basis for NRT�s carbon project, especially on Trust lands - around half the
project area, including all the conservancies in Isiolo County, and about half those in Laikipia � is
far from clear. Sidestepping these serious uncertainties, the project�s validators accepted that the
legislation referred to by the project �establish[es] right of use in support of activities which in turn
support the carbon project�137.
Crucially, subsequent to the validation and verification of the first period of the carbon project �
but before the commencement of the second period of verification � the Indigenous communities
filed at the Isiolo High Court challenging the legality of NRT�s very role in stablishing community
conservancies and its actions of delineating and annexing community lands for private wildlife
conservation without seeking the free prior informed consent of community membersThis case, having been delayed by various legal blocking tactics, is still in process, with the next
hearing due in May 2023.
Assuming NRT even had the right to establish the conservancies or implement the project as it has
done, as the project proponent and main beneficiary it would need the formal agreement of each
of the Conservancies (assuming they did indeed have a legal right to the soil carbon) to enter into
agreements to sell the �emissions reductions� being generated by their respective lands. Nowhere
in the project document does NRT state unequivocally that it has acquired such a right from the
conservancies.
In response to the validator�s question above on clarification of the legal basis of NRT�s ownership
of the carbon, the project stated that �Conservancies are legal entities (certified trusts recognized
by the Kenya Revenue Service) that can sign contracts to benefit from conservation [emphasis
added] over geographically delineated areas..�139. The critical question as to whether the
conservancies had actually signed such contracts with NRT as the project proponent appears
not to have been asked by the validators. However, the issue arose in the context of how NRT
would guarantee the permanence of the carbon project outcomes. NRT had claimed that this
guarantee came through unspecified �conservation easements�140. The validator requested copies
of these, and asked the project to note that �the easements will need to include language requiring
continuation of the management practices that protect carbon stocks over the length of the project
crediting period�141.
The response, as recorded by the validators was not in the form of �easements�, but �Letters
of Intent� to participate in the project, evidently dated around February or March 2017142. The
validators were ultimately unable to determine whether the Letters of Intent or the applicable laws
constituted a legally binding commitment by the conservancies to protect carbon stocks over the
length of the project crediting period, and this query was never closed. The validators noted in
September 2018 that:
�Scanned copies of signed form letters from each of the 14 conservancy chairmen were
provided to the auditors. The letters are in English, and they say that the conservancies
understand what the project is about and why it was being done, including mention
of expected revenues. It further states they are aware of commitments required and
understand both consequences and potential benefits. Item closed.�143
It is important to note that even these Letters of Intent for the conservancies to allegedly participate
in the project did not appear until more than four years after the project had started. Moreover, this
still did not address the fundamental question (which the validators had apparently still not asked)
as to whether the conservancies had actually contracted with NRT for it to trade the emissions
reductions which they were allegedly generating and supposedly owned.Survival International has obtained a copy of a contract which was evidently finally agreed between
NRT and the conservancies. It is dated 24th June 2021. Excerpts of it are shown below in Figure
14. Under one clause of the agreement, it is stated that:
�By preliminary Agreements duly entered into in 2017, each of the Participating
Conservancies authorized NRT to sell the rights to claim the soil carbon accruals and
associated removals of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere that result from the conduct
of the Project Activities (as further defined below, the �Verified Emissions Reductions�, or
�VERs��)144
In other words, even some form of putative �preliminary agreement� (which has not been seen, but
is likely the �Letter of Intent� referred to above) had not been reached between the parties until after
the entire first crediting period, and four years after the project start. The formal legal agreement
between the conservancies and NRT was only put in place eight-and-a-half years after the project
started.
The agreement states that:
�The Parties agree that the inability to demonstrate and warrant clear, undisputed rights
of ownership of the VERs for the purposes of the Project and this Agreement will create
uncertainty and lower the price at which the VERS will be sold, thereby undermining the
social and community benefits intended to accrue to the Participating Conservancies
from the Project. In exercise of their rights to free prior and informed consent (FPIC) and
in consideration of the monetary and other benefits to be gained from the project, the
Participating Conservancies hereby assign the rights to the ownership of the Project VERs
to NRT and authorize NRT to issue any warrants or representations relating to its clear
unencumbered assigned rights of ownership of the VERs��145
By the time this agreement was signed, 3.7 million credits had already been verified and, according
to the Verra registry, more than half a million of them already sold, including 30,000 to Netflix146. It is
not known to what extent the full boards and the wider communities within each conservancy were
informed or consulted about the content of this legal agreement, or authorized each conservancy
chair to sign it on their behalf.The verification assessment of the project�s first accounting period, completed in November 2020,
simply repeated the same assertions made about rights to property and, by inference, soil carbon,
as conferred under the general legislation. Again, however, it failed to question whether there was a
valid and legally binding agreement between the holders of those putative rights (the conservancies)
and the project proponent, NRT.
Taken together, these doubts about, first, the legal basis for the project and, second, the basis
on which NRT was trading carbon to which it had no clear legal right, paint a shocking picture of
mismanagement, negligence of basic operating principles, and woeful absence of the necessary
due diligence by both the validator/verifier (Aster Global Environmental Solutions, Inc), and Verra7.3 Distribution of benefits
It is important to recall that, as stated in the project document, the �new� rotational grazing
practices upon which the whole project rested �would not occur without significant carbon
revenues to motivate change in herder behaviour�147. In reality, however, very little of the carbon
revenues would actually find their way to the community conservancies, and none of it to individual
herders or their families.
According to the project document, up to 30% of gross project revenue goes straight to a Vermontbased company called Native Energy for �marketing� of the VERs148. The document explains
that �To facilitate market transactions, Native Energy will be the listed agent for the project and
will disperse revenues as agreed by all the project proponents.� 149 An unspecified percentage
in consultancy fees goes to Soils for the Future, which originated the project and the VCS
methodology under which it was developed. The remainder of gross revenues goes to NRT;
�Of these NRT will retain 40% to meet project costs, such as for education, conflict
resolution, grazing coordinators, and social monitoring, and 60% (30% of gross revenues)
will be distributed to communities through the NRT Pooled Conservancy Fund�150.
The project document states that �Communities will distribute revenues according to community
decisions, as influenced by community members during community meetings�151 and that
�Payments to communities through NRT will also be used to fund health care and bursaries that
provide benefits to the poorest community members, such as paying school fees�152. This proves to

4.1 Net Positive Community Impacts 4.1.1 Community Impacts (CCB, CM2.1)
The project provided substantial economic benefits to community households, as measured by the Social CoMMs surveys of over 2000 households in 2014 and 2015 and again in 2020 (project). Between baseline and project surveys, a higher proportion of households reported increased income over the previous year and ownership of cattle but a lower incidence of illness. Climate change adaptation also increased, as the proportion of households with access to milk increased by 20% and time spent gathering water declined. Ongoing SocialCOMMs surveys show the project provided benefits to women, as women-led households surveyed also showed the increases in income, ownership of cattle, and lower incidence of illness. 4.1.3 Net Positive Community Well-Being (VCS 3.19; CCB, CM2.3, GL1.4) The project introduces multiple positive community benefits. However, insufficient time has passed since the project start to the current crediting period for most of these benefits to be realized, but here several positive indicators for key population segments indicating exceptional community benefits are shown. First, Livestock ownership provided a clear metric of the poorest 25% of people (Figure 3), and our household survey identified opinions of women, including households with female heads. Benefits were classed as to whether they affected livelihood, health, or ability to adapt to climate change. Household survey questions generally are framed in terms of a choice of 2-4 alternatives from which respondents must choose. Consequently, data were analyzed according to the proportion of households choosing one or more responses to specific questions. Livelihood indicators were the proportion of households that (1) increased in income over the past year and (2) owned cattle. Health indicators were the proportion of households in which (3) an adult or (4) a child had been sick in the past month. Adaptation indicators were the proportion of households that (5) found the grazing program very helpful, (6) judged the quality of grazing lands to be �good� or �Very Good,� (7) drank milk the previous day, (8) found security to be �Improved� versus �Stayed the Same� or �Worsened,� and (9) spent less than two hours/day gathering water.
These assessments were based on household interviews at 2663 households in 8 different Conservancies during 2014 and 2015 (Baseline), and 2,637 households across five Conservancies in 2020 (Project). The results (Table 2) showed that overwhelmingly, across all households, the project activity was associated with dramatic improvements in all three classes of benefits.
Benefits to Women Table 2 also clearly supports the idea that women benefit in multiple ways under project activities. Most strikingly, female-led households report increases in family income much more frequently, perceive grazing lands as �Good� or �Very Good� more often, and perceive improved security in 80% of cases relative to about a third of households under Baseline conditions. Interestingly they demonstrate larger increases in perceived security than men, but men-led households experience sickness less frequently and show larger increases in perceived quality of grazing lands and access to milk under project activities. Overall, the results are highly consistent with strong exceptional benefits to women. Second, the project scenario conveyed numerous financial benefits. Project Conservancies (> 2 years history with a grazing plan) employed 30% more people in total, employed twice the % of employees from vulnerable groups (Figure 6) than Baseline Conservancies (grazing plan in effect < 1 year). There was essentially no difference in employment of women between Baseline and Project Conservancies. Project Conservancies had fewer people than Baseline Conservancies and experienced lower income than the previous year (Figure 6) and a greater proportion of households that experienced increased income (Table 2). Project Conservancies also featured a significantly lower proportion of households that thought security had improved or stayed the same than Baseline Conservancies (Figure 5). Households in communities under the project scenario drank milk at a higher frequency than in the baseline scenario (Table 2, Figure 6) and were less likely to be sick. Finally, response of communities to planned grazing is overwhelmingly positive, as the vast majority (> 65%) of households find their Conservancy�s grazing plan �very helpful� as compared to �not helpful,� �somewhat helpful,� or �don�t know� (Figure 7). This positivity was expressed across households with men or women as heads, among the poorest 25% (largely not cattle owners) and owners of more than 5 livestock, and among people from Conservancies with a longer history of planned grazing versus not.
All these data indicate some positive trends that have accompanied the onset of project activities. Future data collected across additional Conservancies will allow a better assignment of cause and effect than is possible now, but the results suggest that the project activities are providing some social benefits, even as the resource benefits in livestock and grass await better weather conditions with higher rainfall. Anticipated climate change in the project zone is somewhat uncertain, as climate models differ in their predictions of whether mean annual rainfall will increase[26] or decrease[27]. However, climate variability is expected to increase regardless[27, 28]. Increased variability and warmer conditions are expected to increase the frequency and intensity of droughts, shrink the length of the season soil moisture is available, reduce overall mean forage production, and potentially reduce livestock capacity by 10%[26, 29, 30]. Assuming that temporal variability extends to spatial variability, climate change may increase the frequency of periods where pastoralists are in conflict over water or forage[27, 31] The rebuilding of soil organic carbon from the project activities of widespread PR grazing practices will likely induce dramatic improvements in the ability of people in the project area to adapt to climate change. Recent climate trends in the region[32, 33] suggest a reduction in mean precipitation, with longer periods of consecutive years with either above- or below-average precipitation. The principal defense for pastoralist communities against such projected changes is to build heterogeneity in grazing use of the landscape so as to create opportunities for �chasing� spatially and temporally variable precipitation within a season and the establishment of grass banks as a hedge against drought. The PR grazing practices are fully expected to restore perennial grass cover and increase soil organic carbon. The occurrence of greater soil carbon across the project area would result in the following aids in climate adaptation 1. Increased infiltration and retention of limited precipitation in shallow soil layers[34, 35]. 2. Green, higher quality forage available for more months during dry seasons/years. 3. Reproduction by livestock will extend further into the dry season or occur during dryer years, which will supply milk to families year-round[4, 36]. Baseline social surveys indicate that milk available for household use or to sell is available in communities. 4. Greater retention of water in shallow layers due to higher soil carbon[37-39] (Figure 9) supports the advent of standing water in a greater number of places across the landscape to support cattle, which have a greater dependence on water than smaller livestock, particularly goats. These effects are evident even in tropical savannas that form hardpan surfaces following degradation[40, 41] 5. Greater standing biomass and water in the dry season allows greater allocation of livestock to cattle and away from sheep and goats. 4.2 Other Stakeholder Impacts
4.2.1 Mitigation of Negative Impacts on Other Stakeholders (VCS, 3.18, 3.19; CCB,CM3.2)
The principal offsite stakeholders are herders from other Group Ranches or Trust lands, and these stakeholders may be negatively impacted by the enforcement of project boundaries and the perception that traditional use of other communities� grazing lands during droughts or dry seasons is no longer permitted. A key mission in designing planned rotational grazing will be to continue to have negotiated agreements among grazing committees of different Conservancies or communities both on and off the project area. These agreements will allow continuance of cultural traditions while maintaining the integrity of the project. They also may enhance social cohesion because acceptance of off-project livestock will be easier once sufficient grass banks are established.
To this end, NRT has established a regional grazing plan to manage movements and numbers of livestock across Conservancies during droughts or extended dry seasons. This plan uses near real-time information on rainfall in the previous 1-3 months from USDA-USAID Famine Early Warning System (FEWS) http://earlywarning.usgs.gov/fews/ and from the University of Reading�s (UK) Tropical Applications of Meteorology using SATellite data, or TAMSAT http://www.met.reading.ac.uk/~tamsat/data/, to identify areas experiencing drier and/or wetter than normal conditions. From this information system, a large-scale inter-conservancy rotation of livestock can be designed that eases grazing pressure in drier areas while sustainably using forage available within the project area. This regional grazing plan can also accommodate movements of herders from outside the project area as a way to limit encroachment and better manage leakage. 4.2.2 Net Impacts on Other Stakeholders (VCS, 3.18, 3.19; CCB, CM3.3) Community feedback
The carbon project, whereby yet another benefit of planned rotational grazing is presented, has been communicated much more recently due to high uncertainty in the carbon market and a reluctance to raise hopes about potential revenues. However, the Conservancies began on 15 May 2015 and then again on 15 August 2016, a solicitation of participation and public comment period, with announcement and information about the project distributed by NRT grazing coordinators and other staff in the form of pamphlets, and a posted announcement on the NRT website (http://nrt-kenya.org). Responses to the proposed carbon project were made by cell phone text to a standing repository, which was then downloaded.
These announcements were followed by community meetings in September and October 2016, open to all members in each Conservancy, in each of the 13 participating Conservancies. Meeting times and dates were posted at all Conservancy headquarters and were communicated verbally in villages in each Conservancy by NRT Social CoMMs supervisors.
In 2021, Annual Governance Meetings were held with representatives from each project conservancy. In 2021, a Carbon Project Oversight Committee was formed from conservancy representatives and meetings were held to focus on developing additional internal governance procedures based on community feedback.
Information about the project�s participation in the voluntary carbon market (VCM) inclusive of all aspects of the project (costs, risks, benefits and requirements) was communicated with stakeholders through signed agreements with conservancies including, consent and waiver forms and letters of intent. Both of these agreements include language on carbon credits and anticipated revenue including, �we intend to participate in these actions, with the expectation of revenues from the sale of carbon credits, for at least the next 30 years.� Examples of these signed agreements will be provided to the VVB for review. Focus Groups: Wealth or well-being ranking of local or community stakeholders
The tendency in most project types is for �elite capture� and for the poorest to lose out, as has happened with the majority of community forestry experiences (McDermott & Schreckenberg 2009). A wealth ranking exercise should also lead to a better understanding of local perceptions of well-being and poverty, and can also generate a useful sampling frame for household surveys. As described by PROFOR (2008) a wealth or well-being ranking exercise involves the following stages:
� Undertake a community mapping exercise to identify and list all households � Write down the names of the household heads on cards, one per card
� Consult with key informants and focus groups on poverty or well-being categories. In the case of the Nepal Swiss Community Forestry Project (PROFOR, 2008), this resulted in six wealth categories: capable, improving poor, coping poor, declining poor, extreme poor and incapable poor. In other studies, the number of months of household food reserve is a common wealth �numeraire� (note: this stage could be undertaken first)
� Select �representative�, respected and knowledgeable key informants, including some women
� Get the key informants to classify the cards (households) into the wealth or well-being categories . Use of Venn Diagrams for Stakeholder Analysis
Participants firstly cut three sizes of circles � at least two sets of circles using different colored cards. One color is for �insider stakeholders� and another is for �outsider stakeholders.� For each �outsider stakeholder�, the participants need to decide the importance of their involvement in the project, and select the corresponding size of circle:
* Little importance = small circle
* Some or significant importance = middle sized circle * Very important = large circle
The name of the �insider� stakeholder or stakeholder groups is then written on the appropriate sized circles/cards. This is repeated for all �insider� stakeholders using the other colored card. When all stakeholders have been represented, the circles are organized and stuck to a flipchart, grouping and placing the circles according to the relationships between the stakeholders: the closer the relationship between two stakeholders, the closer the circles should be on the flipchart.
The next stage is to cut three sizes of triangles from different colored cards. For each stakeholder (group), a small, medium or large triangle is chosen to represent the degree of influence that the stakeholder has on the project. The triangle is then stuck on the edge of the stakeholder circle. A stakeholder with a small �importance circle� could have a large �influence triangle� and vice versa. The overlap of the circles represents the extent of the relationship between stakeholders (see Figure 5). Once the diagram is complete, it is reviewed by the wider group, which should continue to discuss the relative importance and influence of each stakeholder or stakeholder group until a consensus is reached. For assessing past livestock numbers, the methodology VM0032 requires surveys of at least 30 households, or 10% of households, whichever is greater, in a Conservancy. Surveys, conducted in October-November 2014, solicited the number and kind of livestock households owned, how these are grouped with others or otherwise managed to achieve rotational grazing, and their locations through the year. In addition, heads of household were asked for the number and kind of livestock owned in 2004, 2005, 2007, 2008, 2009, and 2011. Interviews were conducted by rangeland coordinators of livestock owners, typically while out herding livestock, and so did not include households without livestock. This bias was corrected by determining the fraction of households without livestock from the general household surveys, and appropriately discounting estimates of livestock numbers.
Livestock numbers for each Conservancy were obtained from monthly grazing reports by rangeland coordinators during 2014, 2015, and 2016 to provide project livestock numbers for the purpose of estimating leakage and methane emissions. For Conservancies where household surveys were conducted during any of these years, livestock numbers were estimated by multiplying livestock per household by number of households and corroborated against rangeland coordinator reports for that Conservancy.
In total, survey results indicated that exceptional community benefits have already occurred under the project scenario as income, security, and access to milk and water for multiple stakeholder groups has increased relative to the baseline scenario (Section 4.1.3). Further benefits are expected to be realized relative to the baseline scenario as the project continues and more surveys are done.  4.3.2 Monitoring Plan Dissemination (CM4.3)
Each year in September or early October, we hold a Conservancy-wide Project Meeting attended by Conservancy chairs, community grazing chairpersons, grazing coordinators and interested public. This meeting is announced on the NRT website and notices will be posted in major community kiosks and markets. At the meeting a report of the previous 12 months� monitoring results will be presented. Data included are livestock counts, leakage and distribution within the project area, any soil or vegetation or biodiversity surveys, and results of the previous Social CoMMs surveys. Following this presentation, plans for the ensuing 12 months are discussed, with feedback from managers and the community welcomed. An Annual Report of the project, with a monitoring plan modified in response to community feedback from the Project Meeting and a summary written in Kiswahili, is posted on the NRT website. Links to the posted report are sent by text through the grazing management and grazing coordinator network and be communicated via email to other NGO and government stakeholders.
These meetings were held in September 2016 and each year subsequently.
The translation of the monitoring report to Kiswahili will be done after the monitoring report is approved and sent to Verra. This was done most recently for the 2013-2016 monitoring report that was translated to Kiswahili and thereafter shared as a monitoring report summary in 2021. Once the 2017-2020 monitoring report is approved and finalized, a monitoring report summary will be translated and sent to the conservancies. 4.4 Optional Criterion: Exceptional Community Benefits
The project activities will bring considerable community benefits, particularly to women and the poorest 25% of community members.
4.4.1 Short-term and Long-term Community Benefits (GL2.2)
As demonstrated in section 4.3, project activities have already helped increase employment and mitigate decreases in household revenue. Households have better food security in the form of higher and more consistent milk availability. These benefits have been demonstrated for marginalized groups (poorest 25% and women).
Longer-term benefits of improved forage, higher water tables and greater surface water availability have yet to be realized due to severe droughts in 2011, 2015 and 2017 that prevented substantial increases in grass cover during wetter years (2012, 2014) from persisting. However, the proportion of project area in which grazing of sites only once per year has remained above 80% (Figure 9), which suggests that recovery of forage and rangeland productivity is still expected.
4.4.2 Marginalized and/or Vulnerable Community Groups (GL2.4)
Community impacts of the project activities were monitored from surveys in 2014 and 2015 of more than 1000 households and were conducted by community members within their Conservancies, as part of NRT assisted Social CoMMs activities. Data were compared between Conservancies with longer histories of implemented grazing plans (Project Scenario) and onservancies that had just joined the project (Baseline Scenario). These household surveys contained multiple questions that pertained to the benefits discussed in section 4.1.1.
4.4.3 Net Impacts on Women (GL2.5)
Sections 4.3 and 4.1.3 demonstrate that women benefit from the project in multiple ways,
including increased household food security (milk available to drink and sell).
4.4.4 Benefit Sharing Mechanisms (GL2.6)
No revenues have been generated from the project so there is no example of benefit sharing yet.
